docs.title: Debrief v4
docs.text:
Debrief helps analysts turn the record of an exercise or deployment into understanding: reconstructing tracks, measuring geometry, annotating what happened, and producing reports whose every figure traces back to its data.

Debrief v4 replaces the 25-year-old Eclipse application with one shared core that every community uses: a VS Code extension, analysis tools written in Python, and plots stored as plain GeoJSON in STAC catalogues with their provenance inside.

  • Blog: short posts as each capability lands.
  • Guides: the style guide, interaction models and tool-author guide that keep Debrief consistent as it grows.

Development happens in the open at debrief/fuudee. Everything on this site uses unclassified sample data only.

docs.title: Blog
docs.text: Short, frequent posts on what is new in Debrief v4, written in the same pull request as the work they describe.

docs.title: How Debrief v4 fits together
docs.text:
Debrief v4 starts with foundations rather than features. Here is the shape everything else will hang from.

flowchart LR
    subgraph host["VS Code (or the web demo)"]
        ext["Debrief extension<br/>TypeScript"]
        views["Map, outline and tool panels<br/>webviews"]
        ext <--> views
    end

    subgraph python["Per-user Python services"]
        tools["Tool service<br/>MCP over REST"]
        kernel["Kernel<br/>time, units, geodesy, formatting"]
        tools --> kernel
    end

    subgraph disk["Your filesystem"]
        cat["STAC catalogue"]
        plot["Plots: GeoJSON<br/>with provenance inside"]
        src["Imported sources<br/>never modified"]
        cat --> plot
        cat --> src
    end

    schema["One schema in LinkML<br/>generates Python and TypeScript types"]

    ext -- "loopback only,<br/>per-session token" --> tools
    agent["AI agents"] -- MCP --> tools
    tools <--> cat
    ext <--> cat
    schema -.-> ext
    schema -.-> tools

A few choices shape everything:

  • Plots are plain files. A plot is a GeoJSON FeatureCollection, catalogued with STAC and carrying its own provenance. Anyone can read it without Debrief, and access control is simply the folder's permissions.
  • Analysis lives in Python. Every operation is a Python tool served over MCP, so the same tool serves the Debrief interface, an analyst's script and an AI agent. A scientist adds a tool by writing a Python file, without rebuilding Debrief.
  • One vocabulary. Every type that crosses between Python and TypeScript is generated from a single LinkML schema, so the two sides cannot drift apart.
  • Everything is recorded. Each change to a plot is recorded so it can be replayed, which is also how undo works.
  • The web demo runs the same tools. In the browser, the Python tools run under Pyodide; nothing is sent to a server.

The first foundations are in place: the schema and its generated types, and a kernel for time, units, geodesic measurement and display formatting. Three early checks came back positive. The schema approach works end to end; the Python code runs unchanged in the browser; and asking the Python service for each Tote update takes a few milliseconds, well inside the 100 ms an analyst needs to drag the time slider smoothly.

docs.title: Fast enough to drag
docs.text:
When you drag the time slider or a target solution, the numbers must keep up with your hand. We measured whether they will.

The Tote shows range and bearing to other platforms at the current time, and it must update within a tenth of a second of the slider moving. In Debrief v4 those numbers come from the Python service, one request per movement.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Analyst
    participant V as Debrief window
    participant P as Python service
    A->>V: drags time slider
    V->>P: Tote values at new time?
    P-->>V: ranges and bearings (about 2 ms)
    V-->>A: Tote updated
    Note over V,P: next request only once the last returns,<br/>always for the latest time

Each request took about 2 milliseconds, and never more than 7, even with twenty platforms: comfortably inside the tenth of a second.

Dragging a target motion analysis solution is harder, because every bearing in the period must be recomputed. With thousands of bearings, the straightforward code took a fifth of a second, too slow. Computing them all at once instead brought six hours of bearings at one a second down to under 40 milliseconds.

We measured on a development machine, so we will check again on an analyst's laptop before the target motion analysis work begins.

docs.title: Measuring on the real Earth
docs.text:
Debrief v4 measures ranges and bearings along the true shape of the Earth. Legacy Debrief did not, so some figures will change slightly.

Legacy Debrief treated each small patch of sea as flat, with one degree of arc equal to 60 nautical miles. Debrief v4 measures along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid, the same model as GPS, whatever projection the map uses.

The difference is small but not zero. Worst cases, across every bearing:

Latitude Range Range differs by Bearing differs by 50° 1 nmi 7 m 0.09° 50° 10 nmi 70 m 0.16° 50° 50 nmi 350 m 0.5° 70° 50 nmi 430 m 1.1° 
flowchart LR
    old["Legacy: flat patches<br/>1° = 60 nmi"] -- "about 0.4% apart<br/>at UK latitudes" --> new["v4: WGS84 geodesics"]

If you compare a v4 figure with one from an old report, expect differences of this size. Bearing residuals in target motion analysis are the most sensitive: a solution built in legacy Debrief will not show exactly the same residuals in v4.

Every value shown on screen also goes through one formatting service, so knots, nautical miles, three-figure bearings such as 045.0°T, and Zulu times look the same everywhere.

docs.title: Load and look: the whole path, end to end
docs.text:
Phase 1's job is to prove the architecture by walking one path all the way through. You open a catalogue, see a plot on a map, select tracks, run a Python tool, and see its result on the map. That now works in VS Code.

Every picture here comes from CI. A test drives the real VS Code, with the real extension and the real Python tool service, on Debrief's sample exercise. It takes these screenshots as it goes, so they can't drift from what the software does.

docs.title: Catalogues, plots and the map
docs.text:
The Catalogues view lists the folders Debrief knows about and the plots in each. Here that's the sample exercise: three serials on 15 June 2023, built by the sample data workstream.

Opening a serial shows it on the map:

  • BLUE ONE and RED ONE. These are synthesised exercise tracks. Each was imported from a REP file that is kept, unchanged, as a source.
  • The background picture. The grey tracks are real, anonymised open AIS data.
  • The exercise area. An annotation drawn in amber.

The map is Web Mercator, but every line follows the geodesic: the path a vessel actually takes. A straight line on a Mercator chart is not that path (why it matters).

The Outline shows the plot's features, its supporting files and its reference data. The Tools view shows which tools apply to what is selected.

docs.title: Selecting, and the tools on offer
docs.text:
Select a track on the map or in the outline, and every view follows. The tools view asks the Python tool service which tools apply to everything selected.

  • On offer. With one track selected you're offered Track summary, Range rings and Add note.
  • Not on offer. Closest approach, which needs two tracks, waits under Other tools, saying so. Nothing is hidden without a reason.

docs.title: A form from a declaration
docs.text:
Nobody wrote this form. Debrief builds it from the tool's declaration in Python:

  • the explanation;
  • what the tool will act on;
  • a distance with a unit picker;
  • a whole number;
  • an optional time.

The same declaration tells an AI agent what the tool needs, because the tool service speaks MCP.

docs.title: Running tools
docs.text:
Range rings draws geodesic circles around BLUE ONE at 09:30Z. Closest approach finds when BLUE ONE and RED ONE were nearest: 2.29 nmi at 09:21:17Z, bearing 280.5° from BLUE ONE. It draws the line between them, and puts the figures in a results panel beside the map. The panel repeats the tool's caveat, and says what was saved to the plot and what was not.

Every run that changes the plot is saved with its history: the tool, its version, who ran it, what was selected, and every value on the form. That's the start of being able to replay an analysis from its sources.

Track summary gives the start, end, duration, distance run and mean speed of each selected track. Its explanation warns that a gap in the track shortens the distance.

docs.title: Your theme, our colours
docs.text: Debrief takes its interface colours from your VS Code theme, light, dark or high contrast. The data keeps its own colours whatever the theme: red is red and blue is blue, as in legacy Debrief. A check in CI fails if anyone hard-codes an interface colour.

docs.title: What's underneath
docs.text:
• Configuration. One per-user file lists the catalogues you know. The Python services and the extension read it by the same rules.
  • The tool service. Each user runs their own, listening only on their own machine and requiring a token issued at start-up. Tools run in a separate worker process, so a tool that hangs or crashes fails its own run and nothing else.
  • Four tools. The first four are ordinary Python. CI runs them in the browser under Pyodide too, ready for the web demo.
  • Reviewed before merging. Each piece was reviewed before merging by a panel of specialists:
  • security and protocol;
  • Windows deployment;
  • a scientist writing their first tool;
  • an exercise analyst on the sample data;
  • a VS Code engineer and a human-factors specialist on the interface.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• No time controller. There is no current time to follow yet (Phase 3).
  • Bearings aren't drawn. They are imported but not shown on the map (Phase 4).
  • No undo. That arrives with replay in Phase 2.
  • Coarse coastline. Proper reference charts come with the reference tile service.

docs.title: One schema, two languages
docs.text:
Debrief's analysis runs in Python and its interface in TypeScript. Every piece of data that passes between them is defined once, so the two sides cannot quietly disagree.

flowchart LR
    linkml["LinkML schema<br/>the one definition"]
    json["JSON Schema"]
    py["Python models"]
    ts["TypeScript types"]
    fixtures["Shared test files<br/>valid and broken examples"]

    linkml --> py
    linkml --> json
    json --> ts
    fixtures -. checked by .-> py
    fixtures -. checked by .-> ts

The schema describes plots, catalogues, the history of every change, tools and their parameters, and the analyst's display settings. From it we generate Python and TypeScript code; nobody writes those types by hand.

A few things we settled along the way:

  • Units travel with the numbers. A speed is stored as {"unit": "m/s", "values": [...]}, so a file can never leave you guessing. A speed labelled in degrees is rejected in both languages.
  • A plot is still plain GeoJSON. Positions stay as longitude and latitude in degrees, so any GIS tool can read a plot without Debrief.
  • The same examples test both sides. Over seventy example files, some valid and some deliberately broken, are checked by Python and by TypeScript. A plot written by one and read by the other comes back unchanged.

LinkML needed some help: its TypeScript output was unusable, and a few of its Python and JSON Schema outputs disagreed with each other. Each workaround now has an example file that would catch it coming back.

docs.title: Debrief's Python, in your browser
docs.text:
The public demonstration of Debrief will run its Python analysis tools inside your web browser. We checked that it works before building on it.

Pyodide is Python compiled to run in a browser. We ran the same test under ordinary Python and under Pyodide and compared every answer: geodesic measurements, closest approach, formatted values and over eighty example files.

flowchart LR
    test["Same test script"] --> cp["Ordinary Python"]
    test --> pyo["Python in the browser<br/>(Pyodide)"]
    cp --> cmp{"Identical?"}
    pyo --> cmp
    cmp -- yes --> ok["Pass"]

The answers were identical. Calculations run about half as fast in the browser, which is still far quicker than an analyst can notice, and the demonstration needs a few seconds to start.

This check now runs on every change. It also sets a rule for the future: any library a Debrief tool relies on must be able to run in the browser too, or the tool must say plainly that it is only available on the desktop.

Nothing in the demonstration leaves your browser, and it only ever holds unclassified sample data.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Three guides keep Debrief consistent as it grows one pull request at a time.

Guide North Star (draft) Owner All guides An analyst who has learned one part of Debrief can predict the rest. Style guide: language Say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon. Ian Mayo Style guide: theme and UI Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Ian Mayo Interaction models Predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28). Ian Mayo Tool-author guide A scientist's first tool should take an afternoon. Ian Mayo

The North Stars are drafts for the team to refine during Phase 0. Owners are provisional until the team is staffed.

docs.title: How the guides grow
docs.text:
• A skeleton first. Each guide's version 0 names every top-level section, including empty ones marked with the phase that will fill them. New material goes into a known place. Material that fits nowhere is flagged at review as either new territory or out of scope.
  • With the feature. A guide is extended in the same pull request as the feature that needs it. The pull-request template asks.
  • Every entry cites what it serves. An entry cites the principle or requirement behind it (for example PRN-08 or CAP-24). An entry that cannot cite one is a warning sign.
  • Read end to end at every phase exit. Each owner reads their guide whole at the end of each phase, and resolves contradictions while they are few.

Automated checks for terminology and theme-token use arrive in Phase 1 (DEV-10).

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The terms Debrief uses in its interface, tools and documentation. The language section of the style guide says when to use them.

Adapted from DOMAIN_GLOSSARY.md in debrief/debrief-future, itself adapted from legacy Debrief's glossary, and corrected to the SRD. The changes are listed at the end.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Plot. The unit of analysis: one exercise serial or deployment period, its tracks, annotations, sensor observations and narrative, with the history of every change made to it. Stored as GeoJSON in a STAC catalogue (SUB-05).

Catalogue. A folder of plots, sources and supporting files, described in STAC. Each catalogue holds data of one protection level (SEC-02).

Source. A file imported into Debrief, such as a REP file or a legacy plot. Debrief never changes a source; a revision arrives as a new source (SUB-10).

Supporting file. Video, imagery, acoustic files and other content that is not geographic data, kept beside a plot (SUB-06).

History (in guides, provenance). The record of every operation that produced a plot: imports, tool runs, edits and deletions, with who or what made them (SUB-18 to SUB-24).

Feature. Anything in a plot: a track, an annotation, or a set of sensor observations. Used where a statement covers all three, as in "Plot features" in the outline; otherwise name the kind.

Fix. A single timestamped position of a platform, with course, speed and depth where known. Depth is positive down.

Track. The movement of one platform over time: its fixes in order.

Annotation. A shape, label, note or period of interest drawn on or attached to a plot (CAP-03). An annotation with only a time, such as a note or a period, has no position (CAP-04).

Named set. A saved selection of features, reusable as a selection or as a tool's input (TL-11).

Narrative. The log of events from each platform, imported from Word or PDF and combined on one time axis (CAP-19, CAP-20).

Serial. A period of an exercise, typically 4, 6, 12 or 24 hours.

docs.title: Sensors and TMA
docs.text:
Sensor. A device on a platform that observes others: sonar, radar or visual.

Sensor observations (contacts, cuts). Measurements from a sensor, in Debrief usually bearings. Weeks of them may be held as one set (CON-02).

Bearing. The direction from one position to another, measured clockwise from true north. A relative bearing is measured from the platform's own heading. Debrief displays true bearings as three figures: 045.0°T.

Ambiguous bearing. A towed-array bearing that could be on either side of the array: two candidate bearings mirrored about the array's axis. The analyst resolves each to one side (CAP-22).

Bearing error. The uncertainty of a bearing, where the sensor data supplies it. Debrief can draw such a bearing as a wedge of that width (CAP-22).

TMA (target motion analysis). Estimating a target's course and speed from bearings, typically bearing-only from passive sonar. A solution is rooted in a selected period of bearings, and its positions match the bearing times (CAP-21).

Residual. The difference between a measured bearing and the bearing to the solution at the same time. Small, unpatterned residuals suggest a good solution.

Leg. A period of steady conditions. An ownship leg has steady course and speed; a bearing leg has a steady bearing rate. Changes of ownship leg give the geometry TMA needs.

SATC (semi-automatic track construction). Generating a TMA solution automatically from bearings. Lower priority than manual TMA (CAP-21).

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Tote. The table of relative geometry between one primary and several secondary platforms at current time: range, bearing and other measures (CAP-06).

Measure group. A named, reusable set of measures for a mode of analysis, defined by a study's lead analyst. The Tote is a view onto one (CAP-07).

CPA (closest point of approach). The time and range at which two platforms are nearest.

Current time. The instant, within a time range, that every view follows. Shared state, with selection and viewport (SUB-26).

Display window. A period around current time outside which a layer's sensor data is hidden, so that weeks of bearings stay legible (CAP-28, CAP-29).

Storyboard. A sequence of map views, each with a time and narrative comments, exported as offline HTML, a PowerPoint quad chart or video (CAP-13, CAP-14).

Tool. An analysis operation written in Python: Debrief builds its form and offers it when it applies (section 6 of the SRD).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Time. Stored in UTC to the millisecond (SUB-01) and shown in Zulu time unless the analyst chooses a display zone.

Position. Latitude, positive north, and longitude, positive east, on WGS84. Debrief measures range and bearing along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid, whatever the map's projection (SUB-03). Legacy Debrief used a flat-earth model, so its figures can differ by about 0.4% in range.

Units. Every stored quantity carries its unit. Analysts choose display units: knots, nautical miles, yards, metres, kilometres, degrees (SUB-02, SUB-04).

Direction Degrees Radians North 0° 0 East 90° π/2 South 180° π West 270° 3π/2

docs.title: Changes from the earlier glossary
docs.text: Earlier glossary Now Why Times have microsecond precision Millisecond precision; finer legacy times are truncated on import and the truncation recorded SUB-01, EXT-14 Contacts carry frequency Frequency is not imported; acoustic analysis stays in the acoustic replay application CAP-22, EXT-03 Speeds include feet per second Knots, metres per second, kilometres per hour Schema unit enums Track segments: core, TMA, planning, infill Not yet in the v4 data model; TMA solutions are rooted in a bearing period CAP-21 Depth in every location Positions are latitude and longitude; a track may carry a depth series, positive down Schema 0.0.4 World Location, World Speed, World Distance, World Vector Position, quantities with units Implementation names, not domain terms Plot is a collection of tracks Plot is the unit of analysis, a GeoJSON FeatureCollection in a STAC catalogue SUB-05

docs.title: Sample data
docs.text:
The sample data is a small exercise for demonstrations, walkthroughs and blog posts (DEP-08). It replaces the 1995 single-serial sample. Real, open AIS traffic gives the background picture; on top of it sits an invented exercise: a blue ownship, a red submarine, the ownship's sonar bearings and a scripted narrative, over three serials.

Everything except the AIS is fiction. Use only this data in blog posts and interactive examples (DEV-05, DEV-06).

docs.title: Building it
docs.text:
uv run python -m debrief_sample build sample

This creates a catalogue in the folder sample, with one plot per serial. The same seed, built with the same versions of Debrief's libraries, always gives the same files, byte for byte; --seed gives a different exercise over the same AIS traffic.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
The exercise lies in open water east of the entrance to Chesapeake Bay, on 15 Jun 2023. The area was chosen because open AIS covers it, not for any naval use. It is on the continental shelf, mostly 10 to 35 m deep, so RED ONE's depths are notional.

Serial Time Story 1 08:00Z to 12:00Z BLUE ONE gains RED ONE, classifies it and follows it south-west, losing and regaining it. 2 12:00Z to 17:00Z RED ONE heads west for the shipping lane; BLUE ONE zigzags astern of it to resolve range. 3 17:00Z to 23:00Z BLUE ONE sprints and drifts; RED ONE evades, and is not regained after the first sprint.

Each plot holds:

  • Background traffic. 8 to 10 AIS tracks: merchant ships under way and at anchor, a tug, yachts and pleasure craft. Each is named by its type and a number, such as "Cargo 03", never by its real name.
  • BLUE ONE and RED ONE. One fix a minute. RED ONE's tracks carry depth. Both were written as REP files and imported, so they are sources like any analyst's.
  • Sonar bearings. BLUE ONE's bow sonar on RED ONE every 30 seconds, with a 1.5° error. The sonar can hold RED ONE only within 4.5 nmi, outside its baffles astern and while not sprinting, and within those limits contact comes and goes, so each serial has gaps. Between 177 and 349 bearings per serial, held as one set of sensor observations (CON-02).
  • Narrative. About 35 entries per serial, in Zulu time, from BLUE ONE, RED ONE and exercise control (EXCON): intentions, alterations of course, first contact and its classification, contacts lost and regained, bearing reports with their drift, and closest approaches. The log is kept as a supporting file, and each entry is also a note at its time.
  • The exercise area, as a shape, and two named sets: Exercise and Background traffic.

docs.title: Its history, as a worked example
docs.text:
Every plot records how it was made (SUB-18). Its history names each source with its content hash (SUB-11), and each tool with its version (SUB-24). The steps that use randomness record their seed and how each random generator is derived from it (SUB-20), and the synthesis records a digest of the serial's script, so a replay can tell whether it runs the same script.

flowchart LR
    B["debrief-sample<br/>seed 1995"] --> BR[blue-one.rep]
    B --> RR[red-one.rep]
    BR --> I1["REP import"]
    RR --> I2["REP import"]
    A[AIS extract] --> I3["AIS import"]
    I1 --> S["Sonar bearings<br/>seed 1995"]
    I2 --> S
    S --> P[bearings payload]
    N[narrative.txt] --> I4["Narrative import"]
    B --> AR["Exercise area"]
    B --> NS["Named sets"]
    I1 & I2 & I3 & P & I4 & AR & NS --> Plot[(Plot)]

To see the history of a serial, open its plot.geojson and read provenance. Each source sits in the plot's sources folder, read-only; checking the sources reports nothing when none has changed.

docs.title: The AIS data
docs.text: The background traffic comes from the US national AIS archive, published by NOAA's Office for Coastal Management on MarineCadastre.gov from the US Coast Guard's receiver network. It is a US Government work, in the public domain in the United States. One day was reduced to a small area, the serial windows and 16 vessels, thinned to one fix a minute, with military, law-enforcement, pilot and search-and-rescue vessels left out. Every identifier was removed. The reduction and the licence are described beside the extract, in python/debrief-sample/data/README.md.

docs.title: Not yet in it
docs.text:
• Ambiguous bearings from a towed array (CAP-22): the sonar is a bow sonar, so its bearings are not ambiguous.
  • A narrative as an analyst would import it, from Word or PDF (CAP-19): the log is plain text, and it is a supporting file rather than a source, because the builder wrote it.
  • Labels on fixes: REP labels are not yet imported.

docs.title: Interaction models
docs.text:
North Star: predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28).

Worked patterns applied the same way across hosts, tools and agents (DEV-08). Each model is one short page: the requirements it cites, a Mermaid sequence diagram, and a pointer to its reference implementation. Where an interaction is already a requirement, the model cites it rather than restating it.

Model Written in Status Selection and tool offering Phase 1 Requirements gathered Tool invocation and forms Phase 1 Requirements gathered Unavailable capabilities Phase 1 Requirements gathered Undo Phase 2 Requirements gathered Conflicts Phase 2 Requirements gathered Long-running operations Phase 2 Requirements gathered Check overrides Phase 2 Requirements gathered Keyboard equivalents Phase 3 Requirements gathered

Analysts review the Phase 1 models before they are built.

docs.title: Selection and tool offering
docs.text:
How an analyst selects features, in the map, outline or catalogue, and how Debrief offers the tools that apply to that selection.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-26, SUB-27 Selection is shared state that views, extensions and tools can all read and set. TL-06 Each tool declares the feature types it applies to. TL-08 The tools offered are those that apply to every selected item. TL-09 A tool declaring an unknown type is not offered, and Debrief says why. TL-11 Named sets are reusable as a selection. NFR-13 Selection is possible by keyboard.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
One selection, everywhere. The analyst selects features in the map or the outline, and every view shows the same selection (SUB-26).

Gesture Map Outline Select one feature Click it Click it Add or remove one Ctrl click (Cmd on macOS) Ctrl click (Cmd on macOS) Select a range — Shift click Clear Escape, or click empty sea Clear selection (the button in the outline's title bar) Zoom to the selection Selected button, top left —

Ctrl or Cmd adds in both places, as everywhere in VS Code. Shift selects a range in the outline, and does nothing on the map, which has no order to make a range of.

  • Showing selection.
  • On the map. Each selected feature gets a dotted outline in the theme's text colour. That colour is never a force colour, so selecting tracks never makes them look blue or red. Everything else is dimmed.
  • In the outline. Selected features are marked selected. The last one selected elsewhere is revealed and highlighted.
  • In the tools view. The selection is counted.
  • Offering tools. Whenever the selection changes, the tools view asks the tool service which tools apply to every selected item, within each tool's count limits (TL-08). The rule lives in Python, so agents get the same answer (TL-14).
  • Explaining tools not on offer. Tools that don't apply are listed under Other tools, each saying what it needs ("select 2 tracks"), rather than being hidden (CON-10).
  • Unknown data types. Tools that name a data type Debrief doesn't know appear under Not available, with the reason (TL-09).
  • Time-only annotations. These have no position, so they appear only in the outline (CAP-04).
sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Map as Map (webview)
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Outline
    participant Tools as Tools view
    participant Service as Tool service (Python)
    Analyst->>Map: Ctrl click BLUE
    Map->>Host: selection_changed [NELSON, BLUE]
    Host->>Outline: refresh (marks selected)
    Host->>Service: debrief/tools_for_selection [track, track]
    Service-->>Host: closest_approach, track_summary, add_note
    Host->>Tools: For this selection / Other tools

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• Selection state: vscode/src/session.ts.
  • Map gestures: vscode/webview/map.ts.
  • Outline: vscode/src/views/outline.ts.
  • Tools view: vscode/src/views/tools.ts.
  • The offering rule: debrief_tools.registry.applies.

Not yet: keyboard selection in the map (NFR-13, Phase 3), named sets as selections (TL-11), and selection shared with other extensions and tools (SUB-27, Phase 2).

docs.title: Tool invocation and forms
docs.text:
How an analyst runs a tool: the generated parameter form, its explanation, running it, and where the result goes.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement TL-07 Debrief generates the parameter form from the tool's declaration. CAP-24 The form shows the tool's explanation, and any judgement it involves. SUB-04 Values on the form use the analyst's units and notation. TL-11, TL-13 Results may be features, changes, deletions, non-spatial results, named sets or changes to shared state; non-spatial results appear in a temporary panel and can be saved. TL-14 Agents invoke the same tools with the same permissions. SUB-19, SUB-24 Every run is recorded, with the tool's version.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Choose. The analyst picks a tool under For this selection.
  2. Form. The tool's form opens beside the map. Debrief builds it from the declaration (TL-07):
  3. the title and explanation, then any judgement, set apart so it is read (CAP-24);
  4. what the tool will act on ("Applies to: NELSON, BLUE");
  5. one field per parameter, with its explanation and default. A quantity has a unit picker, starting at the default's unit (SUB-04).
  6. Times are typed as the language guide writes them: 09:30Z (on the plot's day), 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z, a date-time group such as 150930Z JUN 23, or ISO. Under the field the form says what it understood ("Means 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z"), so a mistaken day is caught before the run.
  7. Run. Run sends the values; Cancel closes the form and changes nothing. While the tool runs, the form shows Running… and can't be sent twice.
  8. Refused. If a value is wrong, or the tool fails, the form stays open with the reason above the buttons, in the analyst's words. The plot is untouched (TL-03).
  9. Done. The form closes.
  10. Features. New or changed features appear on the map and in the outline at once. A notification says what changed ("Range rings added 3 features").
  11. Numbers and tables. These open in a Results panel beside the map (TL-13). The panel:
    • repeats the tool's judgement, so a figure is never read without its caveat (CAP-24);
    • says what was added to the plot;
    • says that the figures themselves are not saved;
    • offers Copy for each table, as tab-separated text for a report or spreadsheet.
  12. History. Every run that changes the plot is recorded with the tool, its version, who ran it, the selection and every value (SUB-19, SUB-24). A run that only returns a number or table changes nothing and records nothing.

Agents and keyboard users run the same tools through the Run tool command, without the form. The checks and the records are the same (TL-14).

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Form as Tool form (webview)
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Worker as Tool worker
    participant Cat as Catalogue
    Analyst->>Form: Run (spacing 1.5 nmi, 3 rings)
    Form->>Host: run_tool
    Host->>Form: form_busy
    Host->>Service: tools/call (store, plot, selection, values, agent)
    Service->>Worker: run on a copy of the plot
    Worker->>Cat: check result, record history, save atomically
    Worker-->>Service: result, changed
    Service-->>Host: result
    Host->>Host: reload plot; show results if any
    Host->>Form: close

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
• The form: vscode/webview/form.tsx, built from vscrui components behind vscode/webview/ui.tsx.
  • Running from the host: vscode/src/extension.ts (runTool).
  • Results panel: vscode/webview/results.tsx.
  • The service side: debrief_tools.service and debrief_tools.run.

Not yet: echoing values other than times back to the analyst, progress and cancelling a run that's under way (long-running operations, Phase 2), undo (Phase 2), graphs (shown as tables until then), and saving a result.

docs.title: Unavailable capabilities
docs.text:
What an analyst sees when a capability exists but cannot run here, for example a tool that does not run in the web build.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CON-10 Never fail at the point of use; show the capability with an explanation of where it is available, rather than hiding it. TL-09 Explain why a tool is not offered. CON-09 The web build runs Python tools in the browser; some cannot.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A capability that exists but can't be used here is shown, greyed, with the reason. It is never hidden, and never left to fail at the point of use (CON-10).

Case Where it appears What it says The tool doesn't apply to this selection Tools view, Other tools What to select: "select 2 tracks" The tool names an unknown data type Tools view, Not available "It applies to contact_report, which is not a Debrief data type. Debrief knows: annotation, sensor_observations, track." A tool library failed to load Tools view, Not available The library's error. The other libraries still load (TL-03). The tool service isn't running Tools view "The tool service stopped. Run 'Debrief: Restart tool service'." The catalogue is read-only Catalogues view: lock icon, read-only Tools that would change the plot are refused, with the reason. A tool can't run in the browser Phase 3, with the web build (CON-09) Where it can run 
sequenceDiagram
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Worker as Tool worker
    Host->>Service: tools/list
    Service->>Worker: describe libraries
    Worker-->>Service: tools, and unavailable with reasons
    Service-->>Host: tools; _meta debrief/unavailable
    Host->>Host: Tools view: Not available (reason)

docs.text:
• Tools view: vscode/src/views/tools.ts. The wording of what a tool needs is in vscode/src/wording.ts.
  • Reasons from discovery: debrief_tools.registry (Unavailable).

docs.title: Undo
docs.text:
How an analyst steps back through changes to data and to presentation.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 2. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-21 Undo is replay to a point; tools never implement undo. SUB-19, SUB-20 Prior states are rebuilt by deterministic replay from sources. SUB-22 Presentation changes have a local history; view state is neither undoable nor recorded. NFR-10 After an unexpected exit, at most the last operation is lost.

docs.text: Phase 2.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text: Phase 2.

docs.title: Style guide
docs.text:
The style guide covers language, theme and user interface (DEV-07). It exists before the first webview or graphical feature, and pull-request review checks conformance to it (DEV-10).

Section North Star Status Language Say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon. Version 0 Theme Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Skeleton; filled from Phase 1 User interface Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Skeleton; filled from Phase 1

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
North Star: say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon.

Applies to every word a person reads: labels, messages, tool explanations (CAP-24), walkthroughs, blog posts and these guides. It builds on the glossary (DEV-07).

docs.title: Spelling and tone
docs.text:
• British English: colour, analyse, behaviour, centre, licence (noun), metres. Not "color", "analyze".
  • Plain and direct. Prefer the active voice and short sentences. Address the analyst as "you" in help and walkthroughs.
  • Sentence case for headings, labels and buttons: "Add annotation", not "Add Annotation".
  • Name things by what they are to an analyst, not how they are built (PRN-07, CAP-24).

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Use the glossary term. These replacements come up most often:

Write Not Why plot document, file, dataset A plot is the unit of analysis (SUB-05). track polyline, line feature fix point, record, row annotation shape, drawing, markup Shapes are one kind of annotation (CAP-03). catalogue repository, database, index The STAC catalogue (SUB-15); British spelling. source input file, raw file Imported sources are never modified (SUB-10). tool function, plugin, script history provenance log, audit trail In the interface. "Provenance" is fine in guides and the tool-author guide. undo to here revert, roll back Undo is replay to a point (SUB-21). current time playhead, cursor Shared state (SUB-26). bearing azimuth, heading Heading is the platform's own direction.

Abbreviations analysts already use (TMA, CPA, SATC, DR, OTG, DTG, AIS) need no expansion in the interface; expand them once in help text.

docs.title: Numbers, units and times
docs.text:
Display always goes through the formatting service (SUB-04), in Python or its TypeScript twin; never format a value any other way. Rounding is half away from zero. Its defaults are this guide's defaults:

Quantity Default Example Speed knots, one decimal 12.3 kn Range and distance nautical miles, two decimals 4.25 nmi Bearing three figures, true, one decimal 045.0°T Bearing rate degrees per minute, as bearings' decimals; negative is drawing left 1.2°/min Position degrees and decimal minutes 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W Time Zulu 09:30:05Z Date and time day month year, Zulu 11 Oct 2026 09:30:05Z Date-time group military DTG 110930Z OCT 26 Local time, if chosen offset from UTC 10:30:05 UTC+1
  • Put a space between a number and its unit (12.3 kn), but none before °.
  • Times are Zulu unless the analyst chose a display zone, which is shown as an offset from UTC (10:30:05 UTC+1), never an abbreviation such as BST. Never write a time without its zone.
  • Use the analyst's chosen units everywhere, including in tool explanations: write "the window, in the units you have chosen", not "the window in metres".

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Say what happened, why, and what the analyst can do next. Never blame the analyst. Never show a stack trace or an internal identifier.

Write Not Closest approach failed: NELSON and LATE do not overlap in time. Error: ValueError in closest() Spacing must be at most 100 nmi. Validation failed: maximum exceeded The plot changed while the tool was running, so its result was not saved. Run it again. Conflict (409) Imported 3 tracks, 135 fixes. Some content was not imported. Import completed with warnings
  • Counts read naturally. Write "1 plot" and "3 plots", never "1 plots".
  • Nothing is dropped silently (EXT-14). Say what wasn't done, and where to see the detail.

docs.title: Tool explanations (CAP-24)
docs.text:
Written from the first four core tools.

  • Explanation. One sentence on what the tool does, starting with a verb: "Draws rings at equal ranges around a track's position at a chosen time."
  • Judgement. Only where the result involves one. Say what to check: "Distance runs straight between fixes, so a gap in the track shortens it. Check for gaps before relying on distance run or mean speed."
  • Parameter titles. Short, sentence case, and a noun: "Spacing", "Number of rings", "Time". Each parameter's explanation says what it changes, in the analyst's units.
  • New feature names. Name them so an analyst can find them in the outline: "NELSON 1.5 nmi", "Closest approach NELSON – BLUE".

The check (DEV-10). npm run check:language, run in CI, reads the Not column of the terms table above and fails on any of those words in the extension's interface text.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text: North Star: look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means.

docs.title: Interface colours
docs.text:
Interface colours come only from VS Code theme tokens (--vscode-* variables), so Debrief follows the analyst's theme, including high contrast (CON-06, NFR-13). The web build supplies the same variables.

Need Token Background of a webview, and of the map's sea --vscode-editor-background Text --vscode-foreground; secondary text --vscode-descriptionForeground Selection outline on the map: dotted, never a force colour --vscode-editor-foreground Floating readouts (cursor position, scale) --vscode-editorWidget-* Hover tooltips --vscode-editorHoverWidget-* A tool's judgement --vscode-textBlockQuote-* Errors on a form --vscode-errorForeground, --vscode-inputValidation-error*

Native views (the catalogues, outline and tools views) use ThemeIcon and ThemeColor, never colours of their own.

The check (DEV-10). npm run check:theme, run in CI, fails on any hard-coded colour in the extension or its webviews, except in vscode/webview/palette.ts, which holds the data colours.

docs.title: Data colours
docs.text:
Data colours are separate from the theme and do not change with it (DEV-07). That covers track conventions such as red and blue forces, and sensor and annotation colours.

  • Tracks. A track's colour is stored with it (style.colour). On import it comes from the legacy REP symbology, so a red track stays red. Legacy's palette is kept: red #e01c3e, blue #0064bd, green #00800b, and so on (debrief_io.rep.SYMBOLOGY_COLOURS).
  • Tracks. Tracks are drawn solid, with:
  • chevrons showing the direction of travel;
  • a hollow dot at the first fix;
  • a filled, labelled dot at the latest fix, where analysts look for a track's name.

Hovering a track shows the nearest fix: time, position, course, speed, and depth where known. - Annotations. One amber, #c7820a, until annotations carry their own colours. Every annotation is dashed and labelled, so nothing a tool draws can be mistaken for a track. That includes lines, areas and points, and everything tools draw. Known clash: the amber is close to legacy orange (F, #ff9600), so an orange track and an annotation line differ by dash alone. - Legend. The map carries a legend for these conventions. - Reference data. Land is a neutral grey-green at 35% opacity. The graticule is neutral grey. Both are chosen to sit behind the data on any theme.

All of these live in vscode/webview/palette.ts. Analysts review the palette before Phase 1 exits.

docs.title: Contrast and accessibility
docs.text:
Data colours shall remain distinguishable on light, dark and high-contrast themes (NFR-13).

  • Track labels. These take the theme's text colour, with a halo in the background colour, so they read on any theme.
  • Not yet checked. The legacy red and blue have not been measured for contrast on light themes, or for colour-blind analysts. That check comes with the analysts' review.

docs.title: User interface
docs.text: North Star: look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Webviews and the web build use vscrui (CON-06). They use it only through Debrief's own wrappers in vscode/webview/ui.tsx, so the library can be replaced in one place (PRN-09).

Need Wrapper vscrui A labelled field, with its explanation and any problem Field Label Text, numbers or a time TextInput TextField One of a list, including units Choice Dropdown Yes or no YesNo Checkbox A button: one primary per form, the rest secondary Action Button

Native or webview (CON-07). Lists and trees are native VS Code views: catalogues, outline, tools. They come with keyboard support, theming and accessibility for free. Webviews are for what native views can't draw: the map, forms and result tables.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
Codicons for interface actions; Debrief's own symbols for data.

Thing Codicon Catalogue library; read-only: lock Plot map Track pulse Annotation symbol-misc Sensor observations radio-tower Source file lock, because Debrief never changes it A tool you can run play; not for this selection: circle-slash; not available: error

The activity bar icon (vscode/media/debrief.svg) is drawn in one colour, which VS Code tints to match the theme.

docs.title: Layout across hosts
docs.text:
The same layout rules apply to native views, webviews and the web build (CON-05, CON-07).

  • Debrief's side bar. Catalogues, then the outline of the open plot, then tools: browse, inspect, act.
  • The map. It takes the main editor area. Tool forms and results open beside it, so the map stays in view while the analyst works.
  • Forms. A single column, at most about 34 characters wide for each field. The explanation comes first, then the judgement, then the fields; buttons go last, primary first.
  • Messages. Short ones go in VS Code notifications. Anything longer, such as what an import left out, goes in the Debrief output channel, opened from the notification.

docs.title: Tool-author guide
docs.text:
North Star: a scientist's first tool should take an afternoon.

This guide is for scientists writing their own analysis tools (DEV-09, OUT-06). A tool is a Python function with a declaration. Debrief builds its form from the declaration and offers it whenever it applies, without being rebuilt (TL-05, NFR-08).

This is the Phase 1 draft, written from the team's first four tools in python/debrief-tools/src/debrief_tools/core.py, which are worth reading alongside it. In Phase 5 a scientist will test the guide by building a real tool.

docs.title: A whole tool
docs.text:
from debrief_schemas import models
from debrief_tools import ToolContext, tool


@tool(
    name="lab.fix_count",
    version="0.1.0",
    title="Fix count",
    explanation="Counts the fixes in each selected track.",
    applies_to=["track"],
    min_selected=1,
    outputs=["non_spatial"],
)
def fix_count(context: ToolContext) -> models.ToolResult:
    names = [t.properties.name for t in context.selection]
    counts = [len(t.properties.times) for t in context.selection]
    return models.ToolResult(
        non_spatial=[
            models.NonSpatialResult(
                title="Fix count",
                presentation="table",
                columns=[
                    models.ResultColumn(name="Track", strings=names),
                    models.ResultColumn(name="Fixes", numbers=counts),
                ],
            )
        ]
    )

That's all a tool needs. Put it in a module and register the module (see Making Debrief find your tools). It then appears whenever an analyst selects one or more tracks.

docs.title: The declaration
docs.text:
The declaration is what Debrief, the analyst and any agent see (TL-04, TL-06). Its schema is ToolDeclaration in schemas/linkml/tools.yaml. Debrief checks it when your library loads.

Field What to write name Dotted and unique: your library's prefix, then the tool, such as lab.fix_count version Raise it when results would change. Provenance records it, so a plot says which version made each change (SUB-24). title What the analyst sees in the tool list. Sentence case, no full stop. explanation One or two sentences on what the tool does, shown on its form (CAP-24). Say what it does, not how. judgement Any judgement the result involves, and what to check afterwards. Leave it out if there's none. applies_to The feature kinds it works on: track, annotation, sensor_observations, or * for any min_selected, max_selected How many selected features it needs. Use min_selected: 0 for a tool that needs no selection. parameters The settings on its form (see below) outputs What it may return: new_features, modified_features, deleted_features, non_spatial, named_sets, state_change

Write the explanation and the judgement for an analyst, following the language section of the style guide: glossary terms, British English, no software jargon. "Draws rings at equal ranges around a track's position" is right; "Generates buffer polygons" is not.

docs.title: Which tools are offered
docs.text:
Debrief offers a tool only when every selected feature is a kind it applies to, and the number selected is within its limits (TL-08). An analyst who selects two tracks sees Closest approach. An analyst who selects a track and an annotation does not.

If a tool names a kind Debrief doesn't know, Debrief doesn't offer it, and says why in the tools list (TL-09). If your library fails to import, its tools are listed as unavailable with the error, and every other library still loads (TL-03).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Each parameter becomes a field on the form (TL-07). Debrief checks the value before your tool runs, so your tool never sees a missing or out-of-range value.

kind Form field Your tool receives number, integer Number box float or int string Text box str boolean Checkbox bool choice Drop-down of choices str quantity Number with a unit picker, for a quantity_kind of length, speed, angle, duration or angular_rate A kernel Quantity. .to("m") gives another Quantity; .to("m").value gives the number. time UTC time Epoch milliseconds (int)

Units are written as UCUM codes, the same everywhere in Debrief:

Kind Units length m, km, [nmi_i] (nautical miles), [yd_i], [ft_i] speed m/s, [kn_i] (knots), km/h angle deg, rad duration ms, s, min, h angular_rate deg/min (the analysts' standard for bearing rate), deg/s, rad/s

A range rate is a speed. A bearing rate is an angular_rate, shown in degrees per minute: 1.2°/min. In the kernel, an angle divided by a duration gives one: angle(3) / duration(2, "min") is 1.5°/min.

  • Defaults. Give one wherever there's a sensible value; it fills the form.
  • Optional parameters. Mark one optional with required: false. It reaches your tool as None when left empty.
  • Times. A time has no sensible fixed default. Make it optional and choose a time in the tool when it's None, as core.range_rings does with the start of the track.
  • Limits. minimum and maximum are in the default's unit for a quantity.

Every value is recorded in provenance, so a replay can repeat the run (SUB-19).

{
    "name": "spacing",
    "title": "Spacing",
    "explanation": "Range between one ring and the next.",
    "kind": "quantity",
    "quantity_kind": "length",
    "default": {"value": 2.0, "unit": "[nmi_i]"},
    "minimum": 0.1,
    "maximum": 100.0,
}

docs.title: Debrief data types
docs.text:
Your tool receives Debrief's own types (TL-09), generated from the schema. Each selected feature is one of:

  • Track: properties.times (UTC strings), geometry.coordinates (longitude, latitude), and optionally speeds, courses and depths. Each of these carries its unit, so convert it rather than assume it. debrief_kernel.geodesy.TrackPath.from_feature(track) gives positions at any time.
  • Annotation: a point, line or polygon, or no geometry for a note or a period.
  • Sensor observations: sensor_name, host_track_id, observation_type (such as bearing), time_range, observation_count, and a payload describing the file that holds the observations. Tools can't yet read the observations themselves; that arrives with the sensor work in Phase 4.

Use the kernel for geometry. It gives range, bearing, destination and closest approach along geodesics on WGS84 (SUB-03). Don't write your own flat-earth arithmetic: Debrief's figures must agree everywhere.

Call Gives TrackPath.from_feature(track) A path with .times_ms, .positions, .start_ms, .end_ms path.position_at(time_ms) A Position(longitude, latitude), or None outside the track range_bearing(a, b) (range, bearing) as two Quantitys, metres and degrees true range_between(a, b) Range as a Quantity destination(position, bearing, distance) The Position reached; bearing and distance are Quantitys closest_approach(path_a, path_b) .time_ms, .range, .position_a, .position_b, or None if the tracks never overlap series_values(track.properties.speeds, "[kn_i]") A speed or course series as plain numbers in the unit you ask for parse_utc(text), format_utc(ms) UTC strings to epoch milliseconds and back length(5, "[nmi_i]"), speed(...), angle(...), duration(...), angular_rate(...) A Quantity

The geometry calls are in debrief_kernel.geodesy, the time calls in debrief_kernel.time, and the quantity calls in debrief_kernel.units. For thousands of points, debrief_kernel.geodesy_arrays does the same over numpy arrays, about fifty times faster.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Return a models.ToolResult holding any of:

  • New features. Give each a fresh id with context.new_id("prefix").
  • Changed features. Same id, new content.
  • Deleted feature ids.
  • Non-spatial results. A number, a table or a graph, held column by column. Give a column with a quantity its quantity_kind and unit, so Debrief can show it in the analyst's chosen units (SUB-04).
  • Named sets.

What happens next:

  1. Debrief checks the result before anything is saved. A result that isn't valid fails the run and leaves the plot unchanged.
  2. A result that changes features is saved with one provenance record, naming your tool, its version, the selection and the parameter values (SUB-18).
  3. A result that is only a number, table or graph changes nothing, so nothing is recorded.

A graph plots its first column against the others. A number is one column holding one value.

A new annotation, here a line between two positions at a time:

line = models.AnnotationFeature(
    type="Feature",
    id=context.new_id("cpa"),
    geometry=models.LineStringGeometry(
        type="LineString", coordinates=[[lon_a, lat_a], [lon_b, lat_b]]
    ),
    properties=models.AnnotationProperties(
        kind="annotation", style="shape", name="Closest approach", time=format_utc(time_ms)
    ),
)
return models.ToolResult(new_features=[line])

Use style="label" for a labelled point, "shape" for lines and areas, and "note" with geometry=None for a note at a time.

Don't change context.plot or the selected features. They're copies, so changing them has no effect. Return your changes instead. A result that includes something your declaration's outputs doesn't list is refused.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text:
Raise an exception with a message the analyst can act on:

raise ValueError(f"{a.properties.name} and {b.properties.name} do not overlap in time")

The analyst sees "Closest approach failed: NELSON and LATE do not overlap in time". Any exception works the same way, so write its message for the analyst. The traceback goes to the tool service's log, not to the analyst.

The plot is unchanged, and Debrief and every other tool carry on (TL-03). The same holds for a tool that never returns: after two minutes it is stopped. And it holds for one that crashes the Python interpreter, because tools run in a separate worker process.

docs.title: Randomness
docs.text: If your tool uses random numbers, set uses_randomness: true. Debrief then records the seed so the run can be replayed (SUB-20). This arrives with replay in Phase 2.

docs.title: Running in the browser
docs.text:
The web build runs tools in the browser under Pyodide (CON-09). Use the Python standard library, the Debrief kernel, and libraries that Pyodide provides, such as numpy and pyproj. Don't read or write files, and don't use the network. Debrief passes your tool everything it needs.

CI runs the core tools under both CPython and Pyodide and requires identical results (spikes/pyodide).

docs.title: Making Debrief find your tools
docs.text:
Register your module under the debrief.tools entry point in your package's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."debrief.tools"]
lab = "lab_tools"

Install the package into Debrief's Python environment and restart the tool service.

While you're developing, you can skip packaging. Put your module's folder on PYTHONPATH and name the module directly. From a clone of the Debrief repository:

PYTHONPATH=~/my-tools uv run python -m debrief_tools list --library lab_tools   # check your declarations load
PYTHONPATH=~/my-tools uv run python -m debrief_tools serve --library lab_tools  # serve them alongside the core tools

If a declaration is wrong, list names the tool and the parameter, and says what is allowed.

docs.title: Testing your tool
docs.text:
Test with debrief_tools.testing. try_tool runs your tool exactly as Debrief does: it checks the values, runs the tool on a copy and checks the result. A test passes only if Debrief would accept the result. sample_plot() gives a small plot to run on: NELSON and BLUE, which cross, and LATE, an hour later.

import pytest
from debrief_tools.testing import ToolRunError, sample_plot, try_tool
from lab_tools import fix_count


def test_fix_count():
    result = try_tool(fix_count, sample_plot(), ["track-nelson", "track-blue"])
    assert result.non_spatial[0].columns[1].numbers == [13, 13]


def test_fix_count_needs_a_track():
    with pytest.raises(ToolRunError, match="does not apply"):
        try_tool(fix_count, sample_plot(), [])

testing.track(...) builds a straight track of your own. python/debrief-tools/tests/test_run.py shows tools run end to end against a catalogue.
